newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Copper edgy despite China denial of import rumours.
newsitem.headline: Copper edgy despite China denial of import rumours.

text.p: London Metal Exchange (LME) three-month copper could slip lower later on Friday amid nervousness over reports, subsequently denied officially, that China had suspended copper imports, dealers said on Monday.

An official of the China National Nonferrous Metals Import and Export Corp earlier dismissed reports from Shanghai that the authorities had issued a directive suspending copper imports and ordering traders not to sell their copper to hold up prices.

However, he added that at a copper seminar held last week, the firm had recommended traders hold positions to wait for further price rises. But this week it was urging traders to sell because prices were seen as favourable.

Shanghai Metal Exchange (SME) copper futures rallied on the rumours with the most active June contract opening 130 yuan higher at 23,800 yuan a tonne and continued to advance despite the denial, hitting a peak of 24,320 yuan.

"If the Chinese people denied it, why did copper prices in Shanghai go up instead of down?" a senior dealer for a European metal trading company said. "The people in China may deny it, but they may have felt obliged to do so."
But another dealer said he was sceptical of the alleged justification for the measures -- a need to shore up prices for loss-making Chinese state companies.

"Chinese producers should be making a lot of money. It sounds pretty weird to me," the dealer said, adding he found it difficult to believe that the cost of production of Chinese companies would reach nearly 24,000 yuan a tonne.
"It doesn't make sense to me," he said.
"Copper should go down...the only metal which should go up is zinc," a Japanese dealer said.
He said zinc prices should rise in early trade on the LME on Monday and hit US$1,300 a tonne after closing on Friday $10 up on the day at $1,290.

"It is highly likely that prices (may) now push through $1,300, despite the overbought market," broker Brandeis said in its daily review. "The next level of resistance is seen at $1,315 and then $1,325."
Copper prices, on the other hand, will probably open down on the LME on Monday with most dealers in the city-state believing that a further constructive correction is necessary.
"Copper will still probably come down this afternoon. I just don't see prices moving up for the moment," one dealer said.
"Copper should go down and aluminium a little bit down also," a Japanese trader said.
Three-month copper was quoted by regional dealers at about $2,358/63 a tonne at 0630 GMT against its close on Friday of $2,356 a tonne.
Cash copper was being quoted by dealers in Singapore at around $2,416/21 a tonne. The backwardation was pegged at $58 a tonne, they said.
